questions.stem: Which expression is the most formal?

options.text: Abeg, I wan fade.
I wish to leave now.
I dey go.
I'm out, guys.

questions.explanation: *I wish to leave now* is Standard English at a formal level: complete words, no slang, no Pidgin. The other three are Pidgin, slang, or casual colloquial speech, all too low for an official audience.

questions.stem: On the scale formal → colloquial → slang, where does "Give me the gist" belong?

options.text: Formal Standard English
Slang / informal in-group usage
Legal register
A punctuation rule

questions.explanation: *Gist* in this sense is Nigerian informal usage for news or the story. It is fine among classmates and wrong in a letter to a principal. It is not a legal term and not a punctuation matter.

distractorRationale.a: A principal or examiner would expect *Tell me what happened*
distractorRationale.c: Legal register uses affidavit, counsel, injunction — not gist

questions.stem: Choose the best Standard English rewrite of "I wan fade."

options.text: I want to disappear from the camera.
I want to leave.
I want to fade the cloth.
I dey go house.

questions.explanation: In Nigerian slang, *fade* means leave or go away. The Standard English rewrite is *I want to leave* (or *I intend to go*). A rewrite keeps the meaning and raises the formality; it does not switch to photography, dyeing, or Pidgin.

distractorRationale.a: Reads fade in its English photography sense, which is not the slang meaning
distractorRationale.c: Reads fade as losing colour, another literal sense
distractorRationale.d: Still Pidgin, so the register has not been raised

questions.stem: Choose the best Standard English rewrite of "E no easy."

options.text: He is not easy-going.
It is not easy. / The situation is difficult.
Ease is not available in the shop.
E no easy at all, I swear.

questions.explanation: In Pidgin, *e* is the impersonal pronoun *it*, and *no* is the negator. The Standard English equivalent is *It is not easy* or *The situation is difficult*. Reading *e* as *he* is a common trap.

distractorRationale.a: Treats *e* as *he* and changes the meaning
distractorRationale.d: Repeats Pidgin and adds more informal material

questions.stem: Which sentence is appropriate in a letter to the Principal?

options.text: Abeg, the generator don pack up, sir.
I wish to report that the generator has broken down.
The gen dey off since morning, no wahala though.
Guy, the light fade on us.

questions.explanation: A principal is an official audience, so the letter needs Standard English: *I wish to report that the generator has broken down.* Pidgin particles, slang and the address *guy* all collapse the register.

distractorRationale.d: *Guy* and *fade* are classmate slang, not official language

questions.stem: You are writing an informal letter to a classmate. Which choice best matches that audience?

options.text: I wish to bring to your notice the aforementioned hostel difficulties.
You will not believe the hostel this term — the food is terrible and lights go off every night.
Pursuant to our last correspondence, find enclosed my complaints.
Dear Sir, APPLICATION FOR FRIENDSHIP

questions.explanation: A classmate expects warm, grammatical colloquial English, not the frozen officialese of a petition. Option b is personal and clear without collapsing into Pidgin. Over-formal language in an informal letter is also a register fault.

distractorRationale.a: The tone of a petition to an official, too stiff for a friend
distractorRationale.c: Legal-sounding padding that does not fit a classmate
distractorRationale.d: A formal-letter skeleton pointed at the wrong person

questions.stem: Choose the best Standard English rewrite of "She don chop the money." in a report to the bursar.

options.text: She has eaten the money.
She has embezzled the money. / She has spent the money dishonestly.
She don finish am.
She chopped well at the canteen.

questions.explanation: In this slang, *chop* means embezzle or spend money that is not yours, not chew food. A bursar needs the Standard English of theft or misappropriation. Translating word-for-word as *eaten* keeps a joke and loses the meaning.

distractorRationale.a: A literal translation that a bursar cannot act on
distractorRationale.d: Reads *chop* as eat a meal, which is a different sense

questions.stem: A composition rubric says you are addressing the Commissioner for Education. Which judgement of register is correct?

options.text: Pidgin is acceptable because the commissioner is Nigerian
Slang such as fade and wahala will make the letter lively and score style marks
Formal Standard English is required; Pidgin and slang are register faults for this audience
Any mix of English and Pidgin is good, provided the handwriting is clear

questions.explanation: A commissioner is an official audience. The paper marks format and register as well as ideas, and Pidgin or slang in that context is a fault, not local colour. Nationality does not lower the standard of the language the examination requires.

distractorRationale.a: The commissioner's nationality does not change the formal-letter contract
distractorRationale.b: Slang loses register marks; it does not earn style marks here
distractorRationale.d: Handwriting cannot rescue a collapsed register
